quizData.question: Why can an `abstract` method NOT be marked as `private` or `final`?
quizData.answer: Because abstract methods must be overridden and implemented by subclasses, while private prevents subclass access and final prevents overriding.
choices: Because abstract methods must be overridden and implemented by subclasses, while private prevents subclass access and final prevents overriding.
Because abstract methods can only be written inside static blocks.
Because the JVM converts private methods to interfaces.
Because abstract methods cannot accept parameters.

quizData.question: What are the implicit modifiers of constants and methods declared inside a standard Java `interface`?
quizData.answer: Constants are implicitly `public static final`, and methods are implicitly `public abstract`.
choices: Constants are implicitly `public static final`, and methods are implicitly `public abstract`.
Constants are `private final`, and methods are `protected`.
Constants are `volatile`, and methods are `synchronized`.
Constants are `default`, and methods are `package-private`.

quizData.question: What is the rule regarding the 'first concrete class' that extends an abstract class or implements an interface?
quizData.answer: It must provide concrete implementations for all inherited unimplemented abstract methods.
choices: It must provide concrete implementations for all inherited unimplemented abstract methods.
It can defer implementation to its own child classes without being declared abstract.
It must be declared `final` automatically.
It cannot define any new methods of its own.

quizData.question: Why does a compilation error occur when a class attempts to implement two interfaces that declare a method with the same name and parameter list, but DIFFERENT return types?
quizData.answer: A class cannot implement methods with identical signatures but incompatible return types.
choices: A class cannot implement methods with identical signatures but incompatible return types.
A class cannot implement more than one interface in Java.
Interfaces cannot have methods with the same name.
Interface methods must always return void.

quizData.question: Which scenario warrants using an `interface` rather than an `abstract class`?
quizData.answer: When you want to define a common role/contract that can be implemented by unrelated classes across different class hierarchies.
choices: When you want to define a common role/contract that can be implemented by unrelated classes across different class hierarchies.
When you want to declare non-static, non-final instance fields to hold object state.
When you want constructors to initialize base state.
When you want to restrict inheritance strictly to closely related classes.

quizData.question: Can an `interface` in Java extend multiple other interfaces using the `extends` keyword (e.g. `interface Sellable extends Drinkable, Potable`)?
quizData.answer: Yes, an interface can extend one or more multiple interfaces.
choices: Yes, an interface can extend one or more multiple interfaces.
No, Java strictly prohibits multiple inheritance under all circumstances.
No, an interface must use the implements keyword to inherit.
Yes, but only if all interfaces contain no constants.
